narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence, pushing the model strongly toward predicting failure. You ranked in the second decile for Year 3 performance, noticeably below the average of accepted students who typically placed around the fifth to sixth decile. This weaker academic standing in later years signaled higher risk to the model.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 40, it sits above the average of 37.2 among accepted students, giving the model some confidence that you could still succeed. However, this positive signal was not enough to overcome the concerns raised by your grades.

Your first-year academic ranking came third in importance and also nudged the prediction toward failure. Placing in the fifth decile put you below the average sixth-decile performance of accepted applicants.

Taken together, the model concluded that your overall academic trajectory pointed to a higher likelihood of struggling with the bar exam. To improve your chances next time, focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score further, or explore schools and programs with different admissions criteria that place less weight on these specific trends.
